blockKeys: heading�b0:8269a386�Sparse Expert Routing for Efficient Document Retrieval
paragraph�b1:d14fb76e�Wei Zhang, Lina Okafor, and Daniel Ruiz
paragraph�b2:2141098c�Institute for Language and Retrieval Systems

paragraph�b4:6240d57b�Dense retrieval models store one embedding per document and therefore spend the same compute on every query, even when the query is easy. We present SparseRoute, a retrieval encoder that routes each token through a small subset of $k$ expert feed-forward blocks and adapts $k$ per query. On three synthetic benchmarks, SparseRoute matches a dense baseline within $0.4$ points of Recall@20 while using $38\%$ fewer floating-point operations. We further show that the learned routing distribution is interpretable: experts specialize by document section, and masking the top-2 experts degrades only long-document queries.
paragraph�b5:6d6d59cf�Keywords: sparse mixture-of-experts, dense retrieval, efficiency

paragraph�b7:68ea0533�Passage retrieval is the first stage of nearly every question-answering system. The standard recipe encodes each passage once with a transformer, stores the resulting vector, and ranks passages by the inner product $\langle q, d \rangle$ at query time. This design is simple and effective, but it is also wasteful: a one-word query and a paragraph-long query both traverse the same encoder.

paragraph�b11:fa369b03�When only the top $k$ gates are kept, cost scales with $k$ rather than $E$; the model can grow in parameters while staying cheap at inference. The natural question for retrieval is whether query difficulty can drive the routing choice itself.

list�b13:d0d44cde�A token-level sparse router that keeps $k=2$ experts active per token by default.A query-adaptive controller that widens routing to $k=4$ when the predicted difficulty exceeds a threshold.An analysis of expert specialization across document sections, including an ablation with experts masked at inference time.A reproducible evaluation protocol with three synthetic collections of 10k, 100k, and 1M passages.

paragraph�b15:e44705a6�SparseRoute keeps the standard dual-encoder interface: passages and queries are encoded independently, and relevance is scored by a dot product. Only the feed-forward blocks of the encoder are sparsified.

paragraph�b17:a85843a5�For each token $x_t$ we compute router logits $z_t = W_r x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{E}$, keep the top-$k$ entries, and renormalize their gates. The router is trained jointly with the retrieval objective; a load-balancing penalty keeps expert usage close to uniform:

paragraph�b20:6eeb648d�We use a contrastive loss with in-batch negatives and one hard negative mined every $n$ steps. With temperature $\tau = 0.02$ and batch size $B$ the reference implementation, encode_batch(inputs, k), reduces to:

paragraph�b22:d41a1906�The full objective adds $\lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{balance}}$ with $\lambda = 0.01$. The dot product is computed with the same encoder for both towers, so the routing pattern must remain symmetric between queries and passages.

paragraph�b25:2f1cf0a3�We train for 200k steps on 8 synthetic GPUs with a peak learning rate of $3 \times 10^{-4}$, a linear warmup over 5k steps, and a batch size of 512. All baselines share the same tokenizer and are tuned over six learning rates. We report Recall@20 on three held-out collections; each number is the mean of three seeds and the standard deviation is below $0.3$.
table�b27:a2d611bf�Model Recall@20 GFLOPs per query 10k 1M short long Dense baseline 72.1 64.8 4.2 4.2 SparseRoute ($k=2$) 71.9 64.5 2.6 2.6 SparseRoute (adaptive) 72.4 65.1 2.6 3.4

paragraph�b28:41d2ff74�The adaptive controller recovers the small gap on the 1M collection while keeping short-query cost at $62\%$ of the baseline. Long queries pay more, as intended: the controller widens $k$ only when the predicted routing entropy is low.
paragraph�b31:9e1cf689�We sweep $k \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$ while holding the parameter count fixed:

list�b32:b6dc07ff�Increasing $k$ from 1 to 2 gives the largest single gain, $+1.8$ points on the 10k collection.Going from 2 to 4 adds $+0.5$ points but doubles the feed-forward cost.Beyond $k=4$ the curve is flat within noise, so the default stays at 2.

quote�b34:8def56ec�Routing is not uniform across a paper: experts that specialize in equations rarely activate on the abstract. We observe this pattern consistently across seeds, which suggests the router learns genre features rather than memorizing passage identities.

paragraph�b36:e58791a3�To test the interpretation above we hand-label 400 passages by section and compute the fraction of routed tokens per expert per section. Expert 3 activates on $51.2\%$ of equation tokens and only $4.7\%$ of abstract tokens. When we mask the top-2 experts at inference time, Recall@20 on long-document queries drops by $3.1$ points while short queries drop by $0.2$.

paragraph�b38:b1f52bb7�Our experiments use synthetic English collections. The router is trained from scratch, so the results may not transfer to a frozen pre-trained encoder. Routing also adds a small amount of measurement noise to the latency numbers, which we did not model explicitly.
